comparison: Perfect agreement on C38-C43 regarding mutant characterization. Both evaluations confirm the mutations are well-characterized null alleles with appropriate protein analysis (western blots) demonstrating loss of Vsx1/Vsx2 protein.

Both address C44-C47 regarding viability and lethality. OpenEval finds the data well-supported with adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers accepted the observations but noted the lethality was inconsistent with other studies and suggested exploring genetic background effects.

Partial overlap on C44-C45, C6-C7. OpenEval evaluates absence of microphthalmia as well-supported. Peer review initially raised this as a major concern requiring early timepoint analysis, but after revision with 24hpf data (C92-C94), accepted the finding as strong evidence for differences between CRISPR mutants and morpholinos.

Perfect agreement on C48-C53 regarding histological analysis showing progressive retinal defects. Both evaluations confirm the data is well-supported with appropriate temporal resolution and quantification of layer thickness measurements.

Perfect agreement on C54-C55 regarding visual behavior assay (VBA reflex). Both evaluations confirm the phenotype is clearly documented and consistent with visual impairment shown by other functional assays.

Strong agreement on C57-C62 regarding ERG data. OpenEval notes comprehensive data with adequate sample sizes and appropriate statistical analysis. Peer review states 'The data for visual impairment and reduced bipolar function is strong,' also addressing genetic compensation (C63-C64).

Both address genetic compensation (C63-C64). OpenEval finds the functional redundancy data well-supported by genotype comparisons. Peer review confirms this finding is supported by the ERG data showing normal phenotypes in vsx1+/-; vsx2-/- animals.
Perfect agreement on C65 regarding OKR data. Both evaluations confirm comprehensive data with appropriate statistical analysis demonstrating visual impairment, complementing the ERG findings.

Perfect agreement on C66-C68 regarding proliferation defects. OpenEval finds the PH3 data well-supported with clear temporal dynamics. Peer review initially requested early timepoint analysis; after comprehensive data was provided, findings were accepted without challenge.

Perfect agreement on C69-C72 regarding apoptosis in the INL. Both evaluations confirm the data clearly shows increased apoptosis with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis, providing mechanistic insight into reduced INL thickness.

Perfect agreement on C73-C74 regarding RGC axonal projections. Both evaluations confirm the qualitative assessment is sufficient to establish that visual defects are not due to RGC or projection defects.

Perfect agreement on C75-C79 regarding photoreceptor differentiation defects. Both evaluations confirm delayed differentiation and increased cone marker expression. Peer review noted similar findings were reported in mouse mutants (Rutherford et al.), which authors acknowledged.

Perfect agreement on C80-C83 regarding bipolar cell loss. Both evaluations confirm strong evidence from multiple approaches (markers, histology, ERG). Peer review states this is a core finding with 'strong' supporting data.

Perfect agreement on C84-C87 regarding normal amacrine cell markers. OpenEval finds strong evidence from both early and differentiated markers. Peer review initially noted cursory characterization but accepted the data after additional markers were provided in revision.

Perfect agreement on C88-C89 regarding increased Müller glia. Both evaluations confirm the gfap data clearly shows increased expression. OpenEval notes the compensation interpretation is speculative; peer review accepts the observation and references similar findings in mouse mutants.

Perfect agreement on C90-C91 regarding normal spinal cord interneurons. Both evaluations confirm this control experiment demonstrates tissue-specific effects of vsx loss and helps establish retinal specificity of the phenotype.

Partial overlap on C92-C94 regarding early retinal specification. OpenEval finds comprehensive evidence that early specification proceeds normally. Peer review initially raised this as a major concern; after 24hpf data was added, reviewers accepted this as strong evidence for differences from mouse phenotypes.
Both address C95 regarding neurogenesis markers. OpenEval finds the data well-supported. Peer review requested atoh7 ISH data showing slight delay, which was provided and not challenged in revision.

Strong agreement on C96-C100 regarding ATAC-seq data. OpenEval finds evidence for cis-regulatory remodeling well-supported but notes only 2 biological replicates is minimal. Peer review requested additional tables and enrichment analyses, which were provided; findings were accepted though clarification of datasets was requested.

Strong agreement on C101-C106, C9 regarding RNA-seq data. Both evaluations confirm the disconnect between chromatin accessibility and transcriptional output is a key finding supporting network robustness. Peer review requested additional tables showing overlap analysis, which were provided.

Perfect agreement on C107-C110 regarding minimal changes in core retinal transcription factors. OpenEval finds qPCR and ISH data well-supported. Peer review initially raised concerns about tissue specificity; after confirmation data was provided, findings were accepted without challenge.

Perfect agreement on C111-C114 regarding morphant vs mutant transcriptome differences. Both evaluations confirm this comparative analysis is critical for explaining phenotypic discrepancies with prior morpholino studies and validates the genetic approach. Peer review initially stated this explanation was 'imperative'; after RNA-seq data was provided, it was accepted.

Strong agreement on C115-C116, C144 regarding medaka mutant phenotypes. OpenEval finds the intermediate phenotype supports species-specific regulatory weight but notes limited characterization. Peer review accepted the data without challenge as supporting variation across teleost species.

Partial overlap on C11, C117, C145 regarding species-specific regulatory weight and network robustness. OpenEval finds the evolutionary interpretation reasonable. Peer review initially stated the robustness conclusion was 'not supported by data,' but after extensive revision accepted this as the main conclusion with editor endorsement.

Strong agreement on C118-C120 regarding conserved bipolar cell function. OpenEval finds the evolutionary interpretation reasonable with strong zebrafish data. Peer review confirms 'The data for visual impairment and reduced bipolar function is strong' and accepts conservation across species.

Perfect agreement on C122-C125 regarding delayed differentiation and alternative cell fates. Both evaluations confirm convergent evidence from proliferation, apoptosis, and marker analyses supports this interpretation, which agrees with prior mouse studies.

Partial overlap on C130-C131 regarding absence of RPE trans-differentiation. OpenEval finds this clearly documented. Peer review accepted the normal early specification data that rules out major early patterning defects including RPE issues.

Partial overlap on C133 regarding maternal contribution. OpenEval finds exclusion of maternal contribution appropriately supported. Peer review raised concerns about maternal contributions; authors addressed with western blot data and citations showing no maternal Vsx1 protein, which was accepted.

Partial overlap on C136 regarding transcriptional adaptation. OpenEval finds RNA-seq data argues against transcriptional adaptation as primary mechanism. Peer review accepted this explanation based on the minimal transcriptional changes in core retinal genes.

Strong agreement on C137-C140 regarding network redundancy hypothesis. OpenEval finds this well-reasoned based on prior work and current data. Peer review initially questioned the mechanism but accepted redundancy as most parsimonious explanation, with editor endorsing 'yet-to-be-defined compensatory mechanisms.'

Strong agreement on C141-C143 regarding species-specific regulatory weight from literature. OpenEval finds comparative observations well-supported by citations. Peer review accepted this literature synthesis as strengthening the variable regulatory weight hypothesis.

OpenEval evaluated C126-C129 as UNCERTAIN regarding species differences in early eye specification. The interpretation distinguishing between network architecture vs regulatory weight is noted as speculative without additional data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this distinction.

OpenEval evaluated C1-C37, C56 as background knowledge appropriately supported by citations. These claims establish context and rationale. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate background claims as a separate category.

Partial overlap on C10-C11 regarding main conclusions about network robustness. OpenEval finds C121 regarding invertebrates more speculative. Peer review R22 focuses on the overall conclusion about species-specific regulatory weight and network architecture, which was accepted after revision with editor endorsement.
